utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic, are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon. We are ready to continue where we left it off on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Butler, let me just remind you, on Monday we finished with the statement by Nenad Simic who said that on the night between the 14th and the 15th he was in the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade and that the deputy brigade commander Obrenovic was present at that time and that an officer from the command called Ljubo was given certain orders. In my introduction I just wanted to ask you whether you would be able to tell us what Nenad Simic is, who was this officer and what duties did he discharge at that time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, Nenad Simic was a major and at that time he was the assistant commander for morale, legal, and religious affairs of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Am I right when I say that he was highly positioned in the brigade formation, that he was a highly positioned officer in the command of the Zvornik Brigade. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As an assistant commander, he would -- that's a high position.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It transpired from the statement that he mentioned an officer called Ljubo Bojanovic. Kindly tell us what duties did Ljubo Bojanovic discharge at the time as one of the officers in the command of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding - and again it's been a while since I've gone over his name - is that he's also a major. He was a reserve major in the VRS. And he functioned in the operations section of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade. Now, again as also my understanding that this is the person, Major Bojanovic, who replaced Lieutenant Dragan Nikolic at the IKM on the evening of the 13th of July. I think we're talking about the same person here..

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think we're talking about the same person. You mentioned his position as something that I already understand was a fact. But I believe that he was on the 13th replaced by some other officer called Drago Mijatovic. Let us get out of the way before we move forward. Am I right in thinking that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think just to help the translator I believe Mr. Stojanovic said Mihajlo Galic was the person who replaced Drago Nikolic at the forward command post. He said it quickly and I don't think the translator caught it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If that was the case, then -- that sounds familiar. I just wasn't sure. Okay. I can check that over the break just to make sure that the name is correct. I think it is Galic, but I will check over the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we just, for the record, confirm what Mr. Stojanovic actually said, just so I'm not hearing things. I don't want -- if we could clear that up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Stojanovic, can you confirm that name?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's avoid any misunderstandings. I accept what Mr. Butler said about the position of the operations officer in the command of the Zvornik Brigade as being Ljubo Bojanovic. However, Ljubo Bojanovic was not the person who replaced Drago Nikolic at the forward command post on the 13th of July 1995. It was another officer whose name was Mihajlo Galic. So if this is now the translation that you are receiving, then I believe that the OTP, Mr. Butler, and myself are on the same page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and, in fact, checking my report it was in fact Major Galic who took over, not Major Bojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Now I would ask the usher to help us with putting Exhibit D45 in front of the witness. This is a statement given by Ljubo Bojanovic. I would kindly ask Mr. Butler and the Honourable Chamber to pay attention to page 20, line 12 of the English version. We are talking about the statement given by the operations officer Ljubo Bojanovic who was interviewed by an investigator who asked him about the circumstances and whether he saw Dragan Obrenovic. The witness replies: "I may have seen him because he was in the barracks." When we were talking about things, I believe that we did and I can't remember what this was. And something I would like to draw your attention to. I know that on the 14th we gathered in the operations duty's officers room and that for the third time we sent a request to the corps command for the return of our unit led by Colonel Pandurevic. The investigator asks: "Who was with you in duty officer's room?" "A. I know that Lieutenant Colonel Obrenovic was there. I can't remember whether the chief of engineering Dragan was there as a duty officer. I'm not sure. Sretan Milosevic, assistant commander for the rear service, was there. That is that. That is the room. "Q. What time of day -- that was on the 14th of July? "A. It was between 17 and 1900 -- or, no, after 1900 hours. "Q. Sorry. Can you just explain again what time that was. "A. Between 1700 and 1900 hours. We were surprised that we hadn't had a reply to our telegram that was sent before. "Q. How long were you with Obrenovic and Milosevic and the duty officer, whoever that was? "A. Maybe 45 minutes up to one hour." And then I would like to finish with this sentence: "Do you know where Pandurevic was? "A. He was in Srebrenica and so on and so forth." The answer continues: "He went to see a doctor," and then another thing that I wanted to underline. "On the 14th of July, do you recall that you saw Major Obrenovic again? "A. Yes, we were together in the duty officers' room and we sent that dispatch to the corps headquarters," and this is where I would like to finish quoting this witness. My question to you is as follows: Is it possible, Mr. Butler -- do you give us that option that all these witnesses, Nada Stojanovic who said that Obrenovic was there around 2200 hours. Mico Gajic who says that about 0100 after midnight he saw him. Major Nenad Simic who confirms that on that night he was there. And finally Ljubo Bojanovic who says that at 2.00 after midnight I received the order from him and he was present when we sent the dispatch to the corps command. Is it possible that judging by all of this Major Obrenovic was present at the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade at the moment when the interim combat report was sent?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. On the basis of these witness statements, that is certainly a possibility that should be held open. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. My further assistance on this would be beside the point; however, I would like to ask you a few questions in order to prove that there were other officers in the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade. Would you agree with me that it is logical or possible that other officers of the command of the Zvornik Brigade were in the headquarters on that night? I am referring primarily to Sretan Milosevic and then to other high officers who admit that, that is, Ljubo Bojanovic and Nenad Simic, the deputy commander for morale. Do you see this as a possibility? Is this something that is possible?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is possible. And certainly under the circumstances, it would be expected that those officers would be present.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking all that for a simple reason. I would like you to answer the following question: In the military structure, in a situation when there are combat operations and there is a Muslim column arriving towards the suburbs of Zvornik and the detainees are being brought in, if we are right, in the headquarters there, Obrenovic, Milosevic, Nenad Simic, Ljubo Bojanovic and other officers, because this is what is required by the situation, would that then diminish or reduce the role of the duty operations officer and the level of his obligations in all this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Notwithstanding the question on the level of his obligations, because I believe again you may be looking for a legal conclusion that I cannot give. However, if the deputy commander Obrenovic is present in the Zvornik Brigade during this period, it would certainly mitigate any possibility that Major Jokic, as the duty officer, would have ever found himself in a position to have to issue orders independent because he could not reach the proper authority. So there is a link, obviously, between the physical presence of the, at that time, deputy commander and the limits to what Major Jokic could accomplish on his own as the duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to go back to the count in the indictment in which it says that the duty operations officer is a key person in the coordination and communication between the higher officers and the lower officers, the superiors and the subordinates. I am going to give you two intercepts without wishing to depart from our initial thesis, and that is our objection to these intercepts. However, I would like to hear your comment on these intercepts. I would like us to see what the system of decision-making is in the Zvornik Brigade. This is P239, P240. We have enough copies. We can give them to you to save time so we can give our copies both to the Honourable Chamber and to Mr. Butler. In a nutshell, we are talking about the 15th of July in the morning. You've already talked about that, and the moment is when the commander of the Zvornik Brigade is returning to the brigade to the command. So the period is between 8.00 and 8.50, or before 10.00, because the second intercept was taken at 10.00. At the command of the Zvornik Brigade we still have Dragan Jokic as the duty operations officer. Am I right about the general context and the situation during which these two intercepts were taken?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. My understanding is that these intercepts take place between -- roughly 9.00 in the morning on 15 July and they involve Colonel Pandurevic, the commander of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade, calling back to get the situation with respect to what's been happening on the ground in his unit. So I believe that's the context that you're referring to, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely, Mr. Butler. I would kindly ask you to pay attention to the conversation between Pandurevic, Milosevic, and Mijatovic at 0855 hours on the 15th of July. Can you please tell us who Milosevic is in the command of the Zvornik Brigade, to assist the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe in this case Milosevic is the assistant commander for rear services of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And who is Mijatovic in the command of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he is, I think, a captain, but I do know that he does work in the operations section. So he is an operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that both of them at the time are in the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade when they are talking to Commander Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the conversation which took place at 10.00. At 10.00 it is Commander Pandurevic, the duty officer Jokic, and again Mijatovic who are talking. Am I right, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This conversation, P240? Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's 0910, that's not 1000 hours. That's what my copy says. But in this particular context, yes, it is Major Jokic and Colonel Pandurevic and Mijatovic again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The conversation is as follows. Pandurevic says: "Put me through to the duty operations officer immediately." Then the duty operations officer replies and says: "This is Jokic." Pandurevic talks to Jokic and says: "This is Pandurevic. Put me through to Mijatovic." After that, Mijatovic informs him about the current situation on the frontline. Am I right, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that this demonstrates that Pandurevic as the brigade commander, in cases when there is a higher officer in the command does not require information from the duty operations officer but asks for information from the highest-positioned officer at the moment?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In looking at these two conversations specifically - and again going back to the first one that we discussed which was P239 - in the context of the conversation as I understand it, Major Milosevic makes it clear that Mijatovic was -- I believe he said that he knows the area better and he can explain and he gives an explanation. And then a few minutes later after Pandurevic had instructed Mijatovic to call three battalions again, the 4th, 6th and the 7th and report back, Pandurevic wants to speak to Mijatovic again and have the answer, and that, of course, is defined in P240. On the broader circumstances, given Mijatovic's understanding of the situation, it is not surprising that Colonel Pandurevic would want to hear that from Mijatovic as opposed to Colonel Jokic -- I'm sorry, Major Jokic who would be Jokic getting the same information from the operations officer. Within the context of these two discussions I agree, certainly Colonel Pandurevic wants to talk to Mijatovic [Realtime transcript read in error "Jokic"] because he believes that that is the most recent and accurate information available.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I see that in the transcript it says Pandurevic wants to talk to Jokic who has the most recent information. Are you here referring to Mijatovic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either I misspoke or we missed it on the transcript. It is Mijatovic who he wants to speak to, not Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Can we infer from these two conversations that the highly positioned officers of the Zvornik Brigade Milosevic and Mijatovic are fully informed about the situation in the zone of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade and that they are the ones who report to their commanders, rather -- or before the duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this respect -- I don't know with respect to P239 why Milosevic is the first correspondent that Pandurevic would be talking to. So I can't answer how much he knows or does not know, except what's in the intercept. And again, he makes it clear that Mijatovic knows the area better. With respect to Mijatovic, obviously in the context of both intercepts, he is very familiar with the military situation as it is occurring.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will we then agree that this is the officer who is more familiar with the situation than the duty operations officer, because Pandurevic asks that officer to report to him, although he speaks to Jokic first. Because Jokic says -- Jokic speaking and then Pandurevic says: Put me through to Mijatovic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. But again you have to again keep 239 and 240 linked. He does that because he'd just spoken to Mijatovic less than 10 minutes prior and instructed him to call these formations and report back. So I don't know whether it's a general awareness or whether he wants to speak directly with Mijatovic because he had tasked Mijatovic to get information for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So according to the same principle, do we conclude that the previous conversation -- in the previous conversation it wasn't a conversation between Pandurevic and the operations duty officer, but between Pandurevic, Milosevic and Mijatovic, so Pandurevic is asking them for information if we follow the order of the telegrams. So based on that can we conclude that Jokic is practically left out of the military decision-making about the current situation because Pandurevic is asking for a more senior officer and not the officer on duty?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first a specific answer on this one. I don't know that because what is unclear in P239 is why Milosevic is talking and why Major Jokic is not. I obviously can't exclude that maybe Major Jokic wasn't present for a few minutes when the phone rang or any number of circumstances. So I just don't know why the conversation is going on with Milosevic. I mean, from the first line of the intercept, it almost appears to me that he's talking to Milosevic because he recognises his voice; he's the person who picked up the phone. Again, I don't know that. As for your broader question with respect to the military situation, I think that you will have to read these intercepts in context with the intercepts of 14 July 1995 where it's very clear that the duty operations officer is quite familiar with the situation in the Zvornik Brigade zone during that period. So having established that awareness through the late evening hours of the 14th of July, I don't know how you can then less than eight hours later draw a conclusion that he practically knows nothing about the military situation in the zone. So I can't ascribe to that conclusion that you offer, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, that was not our conclusion. I won't insist on this anymore, but I was interested in the military sense. Yes, it's definitely the duty officer is somebody who is informed. That is not something that we're disputing. But you as a military expert, in the hierarchy, if in the command we have such a highly placed officer, the third ranking in the command, the assistant commander for the rear, so chief, deputy commander, and the assistant commander for rear services, is it normal for that person to be then the person who would inform the commander rather than the duty officer. The question wasn't whether he was informed or not, but this, this was the question.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would disagree with that insomuch as knowing that Major Milosevic's role as the assistant commander for rear services and given the context that we're discussing it's an operational issue. I'm not sure that -- he may very well as a matter of practicality be quite well informed. But as a logistician as opposed to an operations-type officer, as a commander I would argue that the people that Pandurevic would want to be talking to are operations people with respect to a military situation, not necessarily his rear services commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely, Mr. Butler. Can we agree that Mijatovic is the operations officer and that Pandurevic, knowing the hierarchy and knowing the logic of things and the military way of thinking, is asking information from the operations officer, such as Mijatovic, and not from the duty officer, such as Jokic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, that is reflected in 239. There is no reference to the duty operations officer Jokic. There is a Milosevic who knows the broader situation but makes it very clear that Mijatovic knows the details of the situation on the ground. Again, the unknown question that reflects around P239 is where was Major Jokic at the time of this conversation? Whether he was present or not, I don't know the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to your investigations, was Major Jokic at that point in the command of the Zvornik Brigade and was he still performing the duties of duty officer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So can we conclude from that that at least he should have been at the command of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. He -- in fact, like I said, all of our information indicates that the morning of the 15th July he was physically present at the brigade command, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we please now look at Exhibit P34, this is the -- P34, this is an excerpt from the duty officer's logbook, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Briefly, while we're waiting, just something that may help clarification in the translation, I believe we've been referring to that as the workbook. There is a duty officer logbook. I'm not exactly sure which exhibit it is, but just if we could -- if it is the workbook with the handwritten notes in it, it would be good for the translators and for all of us to refer to it as the workbook, which is the way I think it originally started out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in order to clarify, because I think both the Prosecutor and I know what this is about. It's Exhibit P34 -- or 534 is the duty --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel repeat the numbers again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P507. So we're talking about P534, I think we discussed this with Mr. Butler on Monday -- we prepared this on Monday. So that is the duty officer's book that we haven't used so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I guess we better get the exhibit so we can figure out what it is. And I know -- it's an issue of translation as much as anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I quite understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just for the record, P -- if we're talking about 507, I've heard lots of numbers mentioned, but P507 is the -- what we've been referring to as the duty officer workbook, those are the handwritten entries that was provided by Mr. Obrenovic. There is a duty officer logbook, which is a more formal document where things are also handwritten. But that has not been a subject really yet of the testimonies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I believe this is the document you're referring to, P534 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now -- sorry, if we're talking P534, and Mr. Butler can help us with that, that is the duty officer book of the barracks, the guy in the guardshack in front. That's the barracks logbook, and I know the translators are having to deal with all this. And I think we'll all agree and it will become clear as the testimony continues.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think now that we have dealt with that, and I think that Mr. Butler has this document before him now. I just wanted to point to one part of this exhibit, so this is the duty officer's barracks logbook. That night soldier Djuric Milic was there. He just happened to be the best man of Colonel Obrenovic. And he notes: "Attendance was not taken due to activities on the ground." And then he continues: "Only the operations duty officer and the guards were in the barracks." I think that you can see this part, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that we're talking about the night of the 14th and the 15th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that then this does not comply with the statements of all the witnesses who testified here, Simic, Nenad, and Ljubo Bojanovic, who admitted themselves that they were at the barracks that night and in the command of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The reference, again, it may be a translation issue, but these folks, Nenad Simic, Bojanovic, and others have not testified here. In fact, there's been reference to their earlier statements, but that certainly is not testimony and I think the record should reflect that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic, you have to be exact on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct. They haven't testified before the Chamber yet, but on the 21st of September 2001 they provided a statement to the investigators. And these are the statements we submitted to the Chamber. So in view of those statements and in view -- now I'm coming back to Exhibit P507, so the duty officer's workbook where on page 30 it states: "Wake up Milosevic and wake up Ljubo Bojanovic." Can we draw a logical conclusion based on all of that, Mr. Butler, that there were other officers and superior officers from the command of that unit in the Zvornik Brigade command at that time.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree. I believe it's unrealistic to expect that Major Jokic would be the only officer or superior officer in the brigade headquarters at that time. There would be other ones and certainly Major Milosevic, Major Simic, and others, they would probably be sleeping at the garrison location; they wouldn't be going offsite. So I agree it's very realistic or it's certainly very plausible that these officers would be spending the night there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. I would now like for you to help us -- it's true we don't have a map here, but I think that you could probably tell us just like that. According to the testimony of Obrenovic, that night he was in the area called Parlog that evening. You know where that area is, so could you please assist the Court and just tell us how much Parlog and Krizevici are far from the command. Could you just give us a rough number in kilometres.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably -- if I have the locations right, probably about -- since it's not a direct route, then probably the road distance around 10 kilometres. I don't -- it's shorter straight line, but the roads of course have to follow the terrain, so I think it's around 10 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We also did our estimates, and it is so. But let's just confirm it, Mr. Butler. So when you go from Karakaj where the Zvornik Brigade command is, then Orahovac, Krizevici, Parlog, it's an asphalt road. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that this asphalt road and these 10 kilometres can be covered in 10 minutes in a vehicle?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In daylight in good conditions, I suspect so. At night-time they would probably be -- especially if they believed that there was an enemy around and they were driving under blackout or maybe without headlights, I suspect it would take somewhat longer. Again, ideal conditions, yeah, 60 kilometres an hour is fine. I don't know that they're going to be driving 60 kilometres an hour on the evening of 14 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that it's always less than half an hour. You need less than half an hour to get to the front line from the command?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it's fair, but again, it's not a drive I've done certainly under those circumstances. So again, situation dependent. A half hour sounds good under ideal conditions, but I have no way to answer that during the days in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. If you take this road, we agreed that you have to pass through Orahovac. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You do take the road -- if you take that particular road, you will pass through the greater area of Grivaci [phoen] and you do actually pass through the small town of Orahovac, yes, sir, or village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that Orahovac is one of the sites of the mass executions and of the primary grave sites of those executed persons?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. On the right-hand side as you're going towards where the front lines would have been, you have the school and gymnasium. And then approximately 4 or 500 metres up the road on the left-hand side you will have the meadows where the executions took place and where the two primary graves were installed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So can we agree that one of those graves was very close to this asphalt road that you had to use?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And while I suspect Mr. Manning will be able to go into greater detail, we know that particularly one grave was very close because, as they were installing the mass grave, one of the houses near the road had its water hook-up damaged by the backhoe. So it would be close to the road and they had to come out later and actually try to fix the water piping. So certainly one grave would be within 50 metres of the road, perhaps even closer. Again, I would defer the details on that to Mr. Manning when he testifies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, just as you said, Mr. Butler. But we have just one question which logically comes from that. Was it possible to pass that road -- along that road and not see the mass grave on the 14th or the 15th? Was it possible to pass down that road without seeing that grave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 14th, the -- certainly during the daylight hours, it would be reasonable to conclude that you could see that. During the evening hours, if the survivor accounts are accurate, the executions took place in some cases under the lights of the engineer equipment and burial operations continued until approximately 23 -- 2400 hours, almost. They resumed again on the 15th, even though there were no more executions after midnight, approximately, on the 14th. So, again my having driven down there certainly on the lower meadow where you can clearly see from the road, you would be able to see that. Whether on the upper meadow, which is about 100 metres up a slope and off to the side a bit, I don't know the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. I have a couple more questions in this area. In your analysis of the Zvornik Brigade, did you notice any elements of willfulness or willful facts by the senior officers, by the units, or by the soldiers of the Zvornik Brigade? Do you have an examples of such behaviour?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Vague and that's a legal term as well. I think properly a specific question could be fine, but that's very vague and it's a legal term and it puts the witness in a very awkward situation trying to answer such a vague question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, us too. We are in a very awkward position to understand your question. You probably could rephrase your question, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, in the military sense, was the Zvornik Brigade an organised and disciplined military unit?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I believe it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Am I right when I say that that was the largest unit of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Am I right when I say that two of the superior officers, Pandurevic and Obrenovic, were young authoritative, very organised, and very qualified and highly trained officers. They were ambitious and perhaps this is one of the reasons why the Army of Republika Srpska decided that this brigade should number so many men.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me break your question into two parts. First, with respect to Pandurevic and Obrenovic, they were very young, they were very competent officers. With respect to highly qualified and trained, within the context of what they were doing they were competent and they were trained; however, just to remember that when the war started, Pandurevic was a captain first class and Obrenovic was a captain. So they were trained formally up to that level. From December 1992 through the end of the war, Obrenovic and Pandurevic, I believe, formed perhaps one of the most effective partnerships with respect to a commander and chief of staff. And I believe that with respect to their combat actions, they were probably two of the most successful commanders of the war. And had it not been for the criminal acts, I suspect that both of them would have found themselves to this day senior leaders of the VRS. So within that respect, I agree. With respect to whether or not that is the reason why the Zvornik Brigade was such a large formation with respect to numbers and units, I don't know that I could draw that conclusion based off of their professional competence. It may well just be because that was what the municipality of Zvornik could put together with respect to forces. Whether or not they were going to break it down into one or two brigades if they so chose to is a decision that I don't know the answer to. I just don't have any information with respect to that. So while I agree with your first part, Mr. Stojanovic, I don't know that the next part of your conclusion would be supported by just that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. I want to continue with this. Did you analyse the interpersonal relationships, and specifically the relationships between Majors Obrenovic, Pandurevic, and Jokic, in this period?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not analyse the interpersonal relationships with the three of them. My observations as to the command relationships and the success of Pandurevic and Obrenovic as a commander and chief of staff are, again, a basis of my reflection of reading their documents and knowing their war history. Within the context of 1992 to 1995, the documents that I have did not lend themselves to me being able to analyse, at least at the interpersonal relationship level, where Major Jokic did or did not fit into that programme, other than his professional competences.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In view of everything that you have said so far about the qualities of Obrenovic and Pandurevic, does it seem logical then that a lower-ranking officer without the career that the two of them had and at the time the duty operations officer would stop the chief of staff of the brigade at the staircase with the words: Just one moment, Major, and in such an address then gives him the information about the situation in the brigade. Would this be contrary to what the rules require in a relationship between the commander and the duty officer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that in that particular context that you've described that it's improper. Clearly Major Jokic, among a number of officers of the Zvornik Brigade, fell into a category of officers who were former JNA officers and because they were professional military officers were certainly perceived to be more competent and higher trained than many of the other officers. With respect to him being a duty officer, logically as new information developing around a situation came to the awareness of the duty officer, he is charged by position with ensuring that the relevant commanders and other officers know that information and can act on it. So I'm not sure that I've answered all of your question - and if I haven't, please rephrase it - but I don't think that it's an improper relationship at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we draw this to an end with the following question: Is it in keeping with the rules and the discipline that existed in the command of the Zvornik Brigade that the briefing between the duty officer and his commander would take place in a different way, in a more formal way, at the command post rather than in an informal way by one calling the other: Just a moment Major. And this all happens on the staircase. Can you please agree with me and tell me that it would be normal to expect that such a thing would take place in a different way and a different place?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, the proper setting for something of that nature should have been the duty operations centre and not necessarily a staircase. So in that respect, the practices or the practice specifically of briefing someone in a staircase certainly isn't normal and there would be much more appropriate settings to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. And please tell me: In the personnel charts or elsewhere, did you notice that Major Jokic throughout all this wartime was ever promoted or -- or when he was promoted, was it done in an extraordinary way or was it done gradually, as one would expect for an officer to be promoted, in a gradual way climbing the ladder?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that he started with the VRS at, I believe, the rank of captain first class and in mid-1994 he was promoted to major. I have not come across any documents which would indicate that that promotion was on an extraordinary basis. So I assume that it was just in the normal course of his career of progression that he was promoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. So, Mr. Butler, his promotion followed a regular procedure based on his term -- on his years of service and the fact is that their relationship was a conflicting one. We are moving on, but I would like to make a correction in the transcript. A mistake was made two days ago and this is done on the assistance of my client, Mr. Dragan Jokic. When we were talking about the 9th Battalion, it entered the transcript that on that occasion, that is on the 14th July, in the morning the 9th Battalion was lined up before leaving for Nisici and that it was Milenko Kajtaz who reported before that line-up. It was not done by Milenko Kajtaz. But one of the officers of this ad hoc unit which was formed at the time. So I would kindly ask for this correction to be made in the transcript. So it was Milenko Kajtaz who reported before the unit that was lined up on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that appears to be offering evidence from the -- information from Mr. Jokic into the record. It doesn't seem like a huge point, but I'm not really sure what to make of that as a practice. If Mr. Jokic is going to provide evidence, he should do it under the Rules that allows him to make a statement or get up and testify so we can cross-examine him. And unless Mr. Stojanovic mistakenly made the name Kajtaz and he just wants to withdraw that. But that's not what I believe is being said. It appears to be a suggestion that this is actual evidence, and again we may have our -- our systems may be what's clashing here, but I would just make those comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic, I think you have to identify the situation where the mistake is made during that period. Because we don't know whether it's your statement or the witness's statement on that issue. So would you please give some explanations about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. During the cross that conducted about the 9th Battalion, I said -- I asked Mr. Butler whether he was aware of the fact that Milenko Kajtaz was the officer who reported before the lined-up unit. So I'm correcting my own mistake. It was not officer Kajtaz. This is my mistake. It was another officer from that battalion. So I'm not trying to do anything good or bad, I'm just trying to correct my own mistake because of that particular gentleman. It was not Milenko Kajtaz who reported on behalf of the unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your explanation. Anyway, we'll check the transcript of that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm moving on to another area. I shall be very aware of the time that you gave me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, in your testimony you also analysed some exhibits which were seized from the Zvornik Brigade. Amongst them you analysed travel orders and work orders for particular vehicles and pieces of equipment that belonged to the brigade. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When we compared them with other pieces of evidence, do you believe, Mr. Butler, that these documents are relevant and that they reflect the actual situation when it came to the way these pieces of equipment were used by the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do. Particularly with respect to the earth-moving equipment because I also have the ability to corroborate that with some of the fuel utilisation logs showing fuel going to the engineer company, as well as on one particular case fuel being put into a BGH-700 loader. So I believe that the utilisation logs for the vehicle can at least be corroborated with the fuel utilisation logs of the Zvornik Brigade and that they are in fact actual representations of the work done.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. We shall take things in a certain order to see whether this is all correct, because we believe that there are some errors there. Can you please look at Exhibit P510. This is the logbook for the vehicle Opel Rekord.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not believe that was one of the ones you had me pull on Monday, so I don't have that with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We have that document if it's needed. I don't believe it's an engineering document; I think it's a military police document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. This is the document you're referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Butler. I would just like to confirm something with you. This is a vehicle used by the military police. It's an Opel Rekord. You said on the 13th of July it travelled 209 kilometres. You analysed this and you said that amongst other places the vehicle went to the Standard IKM Zvornik, Lokanj and then there is an entry: Standard, Bratunac, Zvornik. Can you please tell us in your analysis, did you arrive at a conclusion that this vehicle went to Bratunac at all, and if it did, at what time did it go to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The log itself does not indicate at what time that vehicle went to Bratunac. There are, I believe, two witness statements that indicate that this vehicle did go sometime on the 13th, I'm just not sure whether -- I believe it may be in the late afternoon hours. I believe that according to at least one of the statements, this vehicle was used to escort the UN convoy that had crossed over at Zvornik down to Bratunac and then it returned. So I believe that if in fact this vehicle was used for that, that that would be in the late afternoon hours of 13 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. We shall continue to explore this. Now can we look at P516. This is the logbook for the engineering vehicle Skip Torpedo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojanovic, could we have our break and then come back to look at that document? Yes, we'll resume until 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Before the break we started talking about P516 and the vehicle in question is Skip Torpedo. According to the logbook you will agree with me that this vehicle was in Orahovac, it was digging a trench in Orahovac. Am I right in thinking that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That is what is listed on 14 July. Is that correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On page 1 it says that the co-driver or two co-drivers were Cvijetin Ristanovic and Milos Mitrovic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that Cvijetin Ristanovic also conducted a machine called BGH-700 and that on that same day he was also in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that from the document because we don't have a utilisation log for the BGH-700, so I can't draw that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Shall we look at the statement given by Milos Mitrovic and see what he has to say about that. Can we ask the usher to help us with this Exhibit D46/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to using the statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In the manner stated by the witness just to see what he says about it. A paraphrased question about Mr. Butler -- Mitrovic says he was or was not there, now did you fit this into your analysis. But just to go through and again read something without it being an impeachment or to refresh the recollection for a particular purpose is not proper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, could you inform us what is the purpose of using this statement? I understand you have to request a question to this witness. If there is any difference, you may use certain documents to rebut the statement of this witness. But first of all you have to put your question first to this witness. Maybe the answer of this witness will be agreeable to your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at the beginning I asked Mr. Butler whether he thought that these documents were relevant and correct; Mr. Butler said yes. As a matter of principle, I can't say definitely, but that these documents are not correct. I would just like to confront the key players with what Mr. Butler said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: (redacted). It seems to me that this is a good opportunity to confront Mr. Butler with this witness statement in order to prove the relevance of this document and what this witness is actually going to say, because we will not have another opportunity to examine Mr. Butler. I just want to show him one sentence. What I'm saying, Your Honour, is that according to what we have - and I'm not talking about any tricks in my questions - this piece of equipment did not work in Orahovac on the 14th of July. It was the machine called BGH-70 [as interpreted] and the Skip torpedo wasn't there. You already had the testimonies of the two survivors from Orahovac who described those two machines, but I would like Mr. Butler to tell us something about that. I'm not implying that the work log is either correct or not correct. So this is my only thesis that I would like to confront Mr. Butler with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: One clarification is that BGH-70 or -700?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the name of the equipment is BGH-700, BGH-700. And this piece of equipment was there on the 14th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed and we'll see how far you can go.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, can you please look at page 17, line 8 of the English version. This is a witness, one of the two who were released from Snagovo on the 14th and returned to the engineering company. The witness's name is Milos Mitrovic. He is asked by the OTP official: "According to the work log, it transpires that you were the driver of the Torpedo." And Milos Mitrovic answered: "Yes, but I didn't go anywhere on the 14th and the 15th. "Q. According to the logbook, you went from the base to Orahovac and back on the 14th to do some digging? The answer: "No. "Q. Would you like to look at this logbook? "A. Yes, let me do that." He is shown the logbook. And the witness says: "The Skip didn't go to Orahovac on the 14th and the 15th. The only possibility I can see here is that fuel was requested for this piece of equipment. There were other pieces of equipment whose journey was not accompanied by the logbook." The next question is: "We have the logbooks of all the other vehicles that you have mentioned earlier today." And the witness answers: "Yes, I know, but what I'm saying is the truth. There are other witnesses who can prove whether I was in Orahovac or not. I was not in Orahovac and this piece of equipment was not in Orahovac." And now my question to you, sir: Mr. Butler, is it true what this witness is saying or is the truth contained in the work log? What did you learn in the course of your analysis?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Asking Mr. Butler just to testify about the truth of a witness in this context is really not relevant. He can compare documents and statements, but -- I wish all of us had the secret to the truth, but that's not a relevant question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojanovic, you may rephrase your question by asking Mr. Butler to make some comments on these kind of statements in this document and you could point out that there are some conflicts between this witness's testimony and what he said here. But whether it's true or not is another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, you have both situations in front of you. You are a military expert, can you help us, please. According to your analysis, what really happened with the Skip equipment? Was the thing that happened something that is entered in the logbook or, on the contrary, was it what this person had to say about it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe in this respect that the annotations in the logbook -- I see no reason for them not to be accurate. Trying to put -- trying to just spin this around from the completely different version, if we were to assume the witness statement in this respect is accurate, it raises the question: Why if the vehicle wasn't there and if the vehicle wasn't in use would somebody on 14 July note it that it was? Certainly this particular document corresponds with the preponderance of information that we've developed with respect to the engineer equipment and the fuel and survivor statements. So, I mean certainly in this respect I believe that the document is the most accurate reflection of the vehicle's use that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. I believe that the question that you have just raised was also raised by the investigator. The investigator questioned the annotation in the logbook and the witness answered: This was done to obtain fuel. Secondly, the survivors that we heard today explained that there were two pieces of equipment, one was the backhoe excavator and the other was a backhoe loader; both were yellow pieces of equipment. However, I'm going to accept your allegation that the witness did not say the truth and that the document is correct. However, I believe that this piece of equipment was not in Orahovac. Can you please look at P517; this is the logbook for the vehicle TAM 75.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can interject for one second as to your last comment, just to be clear, I never made an allegation as to whether or not the witness said the truth or not. I stand by the document insomuch as I believe that the bulk of evidence that we have supports that. But I'm not raising a value judgement one way or the other as to the truthfulness of a witness, certainly one that will appear before this Trial Chamber, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: However, you will agree with me that the two are mutually exclusive?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly with respect to the document and this individual's explanation, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Then can you also agree with me that in the record of fuel that was issued, the Skip Torpedo was not noted down but fuel was issued to another vehicle?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular document - and we're back on 516, Prosecution Exhibit 516 - it indicates that 40 litres of fuel were designated for this vehicle. I have no way of knowing if that fuel was diverted for any reason. So I mean in that respect, I mean, the document says what it says. It is consistent with the other information, and I -- again, unless the argument is going to be that they're diverting the fuel for blackmarket reasons or something else, I would be questioning why they would be putting the fuel here on this vehicle and not actually putting it into the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Could we now look at P517, Mr. Butler. Thank you, I'm satisfied with your answer. In this exhibit, 517, the vehicle workbook for the TAM 75 vehicle, according to the logbook the vehicle was operated by Ostoja Stojanovic. Am I correct, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is the name of the individual listed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Also it states that this vehicle and this driver on the 14th of July went -- it says here went several times from the base to Orahovac and back to base on the 14th of July and that is how you also commented on this particular document. Is that correct, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, could we now go back to our Exhibit 40 in order to identify the statement by Ostoja Stojanovic. If you don't have a copy here, I can provide you with a copy in English just so that we can cover this document as quickly as possible. So the statement of Ostoja Stojanovic, could the usher please give the document to the witness. We used this exhibit, if you remember, when we were talking about resubordination and also the Kravica warehouse. Could you please look at page 6, line 15 to 17 in the English version. The investigator tells the witness, who has been indicated in the vehicle workbook as the driver and says: "Is it true that you drove a truck to Orahovac?" And the driver replies: "No, I didn't go to Orahovac with the truck either. What truck is that? Does it say there what truck it is?" The Prosecutor says: "It's TAM 75, licence plates M-5264." And the -- replies: "That is not true that between the hours of 7.00 a.m. in the morning and midnight you were driving for the army from the base to Orahovac to the base to Orahovac, to the base to Orahovac" and so on. The interviewee says: "No, no, that is not true. I did not drive it." And he says that on page 7, line 7. He says he went to the civilian protection in Zvornik and then later from the Bratunac Territorial Defence to the Kravica warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: (redacted). What does your investigation indicate, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, in this respect, the document says what it says. Certainly with respect to drivers, I hold open the possibility, particularly with trucks or general-purpose vehicles of this nature, that another individual may have driven the vehicle that day who wasn't the listed driver. The normal practice would have been if that new individual was driving the vehicle, as we've seen on a number of occasions, he will handwrite his name as the operator. That I believe, if we look at the B/C/S, you don't have that. What you also have - and perhaps while I'm not sure how much of an assistance it is - is on the B/C/S version you will have signatures of various individuals. And I'm not in a position to be able to tell the Trial Chamber whose signature it is on any given day, unfortunately. So I certainly hold open the possibility that in this respect that the driver may very well be different; however, with respect to drivers as opposed to with respect to the actual utilisation of the vehicle, I would put that in a different category. The final note I would like to make on the issue of drivers is that while I hold this possibility open for a standard vehicle driver, such as the driver of a TAM 75, I would not necessarily hold that possibility open for heavy equipment operators who require more specialised knowledge of the vehicles. Presumably vehicles like that are not vehicles that your average soldier can get in and operate without any form of experience or training. Whereas, in a TAM 75, you can make that inference that somebody else could.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, Mr. Butler, you are giving us the option that this vehicle work log may not reflect the truth or may not be giving the correct driver's name. Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I noted that while the practice was that the driver would, in fact, put down in handwritten form his name, I do hold open the possibility that perhaps a particular driver didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Could we now look at Exhibit P522, and this is the work -- vehicle work log for ULT-220.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe I have that document, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please ask the usher to give my copy in B/C/S to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree, Mr. Butler, with the fact that according to this vehicle work log, ULT-220 belongs to the Birac Holding company?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That is what it indicates in the -- or on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the same document, it says that Veljko Kovacevic operated this equipment. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that there is no need, but if you want we could perhaps look at this together. Would you agree with me that according to the list of the engineers' unit - and this is Exhibit P514 - the name of Veljko Kovacevic is not mentioned in the list?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe I have testified as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would just like you to confirm that this machine does not belong to the engineers and is not on the list of the Zvornik Brigade engineering equipment and that this soldier is not a member of the Zvornik Brigade. So the machine operator and driver are not members of the Zvornik Brigade. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. In this particular instance, the machine belongs to a civilian construction firm. The driver is not listed as a member of the engineer company. And the only reason why I suspect we would have a vehicle log like this is for the accounting of the fuel that the army had put in the vehicle when they requisitioned its use.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely, Mr. Butler. Thank you very much. I will not insist on this any longer. We say that the ULT-220 does not belong to the engineers' company and it's in the list in order to account for the fuel. But another question: Who makes these vehicle work log books? And whose signature is at the bottom of these pages? Who fills these sheets in and does that have anything to do with the engineers' unit?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The actual issue on the sheets of accountability are done out of an organ of the rear services department of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade. What we found was that these records are compiled by the rear services branch, and what we actually found when we went through the records was a possibly 3- or 4-inch stack that was bound together of all the documents were July 1995 which represent the vehicle work logs of the entire brigade for that month. So these were not found separately, they were found in a bundle with all of the vehicle logs for the Zvornik Infantry Brigade. I believe that the process was that at the end of the month when these sheets were turned in and new ones were issued -- or in some cases when the sheet was filled in completely and the new one was issued in mid-month, what happened afterward is it would be the rear services branch function to audit this to ensure proper consumption of fuel, miles, and things of that nature. So again, the purpose of these log sheets are primarily for auditing after the fact in order to account for fuel, time, and other variables that military organisations would have to track.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So in that context, just one question: Am I right if I said that the issuance of fuel and accounting for it was also something that the rear services were responsible for and not the engineers' unit?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct. Fuel distribution and accountability thereof is a rear services branch function, not an engineering branch function.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Can we now look at Exhibit P513; it's the daily order of the commander of the engineers' unit for the 14th of July, 1995. Mr. Butler, I just wanted to clarify one thing. In your examination-in-chief you spoke about this document and you said that it is correct that in this daily order there are no instructions for the work of the engineering machinery in Orahovac on the 14th. And if I recall correctly, you interpreted that by the fact that the daily order was written in the morning and it was not known that the machinery would be used in Orahovac in the afternoon. Have I paraphrased you correctly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not known by the people who wrote this orders book in the morning; that is correct, sir; that is what I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is exactly why I wanted to show you this document. Can you conclude on the basis of this document that practically on the 14th in the morning hours the engineering company did not know what would be happening and whether their machinery would be required to be used?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in this respect -- let's go back to what we talked about earlier on qualifying the engineer company. At that time it was the deputy and perhaps three or four people left it at the company headquarters. The bulk of the people were either on operational deployments, either outside of the Zvornik sector or, in the case of the company commander and his group of 15 engineers, inside the Zvornik area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I received the translation that the deputy company commander left. If I'm not mistaken, the commander went and the deputy commander was at the command on the 14th. Am I correct in that, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Am I correct then that -- in saying that the engineering company in the morning hours of the 14th had no plan about what their machinery would be doing on the afternoon of the 14th?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe that's the proper inference that can be drawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Just one more thing here. In the introductory part of your report, which we titled Narrative About the Military Events in Srebrenica, under item 7.78, I'm paraphrasing, you said that the task of the rear services is to ensure the intake the security of the military -- of the prisoners of war, so the rear services of the Zvornik Brigade actually did not make any preparations to accept such a number of prisoners of war. I'm paraphrasing you, so I hope that I did this correctly. Did I paraphrase you correctly, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In paragraph 7.78 of my narrative, I make the observation that from the survivor accounts at the schools in the Zvornik Brigade zone where Muslim prisoners were held, there was apparently no provisions made for what I call life support for these individuals. There was very little water, and only that water that was available at the school itself. There was no food. Sanitation was limited, and there was no noted medical support for the prisoners. Now, keeping that in mind, and again reflecting back to the brigade rules, those are within the purview of the Zvornik Brigade or any brigade's rear services branch to make those things happen. Those are logistical functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested precisely in that context. It's obvious that nothing -- no preparations were made by the rear services of the Zvornik Brigade. So can we draw the conclusion from that that the rear or the rear units of the Zvornik Brigade practically had no information about the arrival of such a number of prisoners of war to the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade on the 14th in the morning?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is one interpretation. Certainly the other interpretation would be that there was an awareness, and given the fact that everyone within the brigade leadership knew that the prisoners were going to be killed, there did not seem to be a reason why you would provide these. As I noted in my paragraph 7.78, there were select food deliveries that we know were made to the military police at Orahovac. When you examine the accounts of the crime scenes from some of the survivors where they talk about a process where their hands were bound with ligatures or wire that came from certain locations that the investigation has worked on - I don't know all the mechanics of those - certainly some logistical provisions to at least facilitate the execution and burial process were being made. So while I do hold open the possibility that you have suggested, that it was because they were unaware of the numbers of the prisoners that were coming in, I believe that in the face of the majority of the evidence that the most reasonable conclusion is that there was an awareness of the numbers of the prisoners and there was just no effort made because everyone knew within the senior leadership of the brigade that these people were going to be executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, do you have any arguments or any document which would indicate that information came from Obrenovic about what would happen, that this information came to Milosevic as his assistant for logistics. Or is this something that is still in the sphere of an assumption?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I have no documents that would reflect that Obrenovic informed Major Milosevic or Captain Milosevic, I believe, with respect to that particular issue. The only document that we have within that time frame is the 15 July interim combat report where Colonel Pandurevic notes the presence of prisoners in the schools.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is what I actually wanted to talk about, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please show the witness Exhibit D51 in which we used the term "secret command of troops," because we also think the same as you do. There is no public document about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we please look at this term "secret command or commanding of troops," which implies the clandestine relay of orders, combat commandments and reports in the course of interaction between higher and lower commands. And then it goes on to say how this has effected the use of coded card, coded conversation, manual secret names of commands and so on and so forth. Would you agree with me, Mr. Butler, that this, I would say, significant movement and crime of such a scale would not be something that would be conveyed through the usual channels of issuing orders but would more likely be done through the secret chain of command, the way it was described in the military lexicon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I object to the form of that question. There's no -- it misstates the facts. There's no discussion of a secret chain of command in the military lexicon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stojanovic, I think you have to establish that the secret commanding of troops existed in that particular unit. Then you may ask this question to this witness, or you may first ask this witness whether he's familiar with this term or not. Then begin your questions on more substantive matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, are you familiar in military terminology with the concept of secret command, and did you encounter such a term in all of the events relating to the Srebrenica operation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The term of art as I understand it from this particular document or lexicon is with respect to the ability to pass orders in such a manner to ensure the secrecy of those orders is maintained. In some particular cases, we see manifestations of that with respect to particularly the intercepts, where subscribers on those intercepts indicate that there are things that are being talked about on those lines that should not be talked about. So that, I believe, is one aspect of this particular definition. The other relaying of orders in this context, I believe that a number of witnesses have testified that -- or at least certainly one that I'm aware of has testified that he physically went himself to relay orders with respect to the movements of prisoners rather than risk putting that information out over a means that could be intercepted. And certainly with that respect, by doing that you certainly do narrow down the circle of people who might potentially know, either by design or communications clerks or other individuals who because of their duty the message would be passed through them to the recipient. So in that respect I do believe that we have seen manifestations of that clandestine way of passing orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Butler. This is exactly what I wanted to hear from you. I want you to make an inference and agree with me that this operation did imply a certain degree of secrecy, at least during its first stages, and that this information was kept within an inner circle of officers who were in charge of carrying out the operation.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to the movement of the Muslim prisoners from the Bratunac area to Zvornik, I believe that as the evidence has been laid out it does indicate that initially it was a very small circle of officers. However, I also believe that as you look at how it unfolds over time, what you start seeing, almost on an exponential basis, is that as other parties become involved in the process, you have a rapidly growing issue of awareness of at least parts of what is going on. So in that respect, I agree; initially it was a very small circle, but it was not very long that given the volume of prisoners that were coming in and the varied up to five locations that they were being stored at, it rapidly became an issue that a lot of the members of the brigade became aware of, both at the headquarters and at the battalions where these facilities were located and whose troops were in some respects expected to guard them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Just for the record, I would like to repeat that this is D51, however this is D58. That's how we have identified this exhibit. Thank you. Let's now look at one part of what you have already talked about when questioned by Mr. Karnavas. The transcript is dated the 18th of November. Let's comment on some parts of this particular part of your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the usher to help us to present the relevant part of the transcript. We have identified it as D51/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, this is the cross-examination which took place on the 18th of November. I'm going to read the relevant parts of the transcript. Mr. Karnavas asked you: "After the sweep operation, one would expect if there has been battle in that area that there would be also asanacija." Your answer is: "Generally once the area is secured that would be an expectation, yes. "Q. Those two functions which go hand in glove after an operation are proper military functions?" Your answer was: "Yes, sir, they are." Do you remember this part of the cross-examination, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My question to you is as follows: When you say "asanacija," and this term is very often mentioned in the documents of the main corps and the Drina Corps and in the command of the Zvornik Brigade, is it mentioned often, this term?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there are two references to this specific term. One of them is the 15 July interim combat report by Colonel Pandurevic, and the other one is a notation in the Bratunac Brigade command meetings logbook on, I believe it's either late September or early October, where Captain First Class Momir Nikolic uses that phrase with respect to a task from the Main Staff. I don't believe that I have seen it in other documents with respect to what we're talking about with Srebrenica; however, I have seen the term used in other documents within the context of the larger war where it's used as well. So I hope I've answered the question on that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you have indeed, Mr. Butler. Although I have prepared an exhibit, P539, which is an order of the Main Staff, and it's item 5. It calls for the asanacija of the entire battlefield and the terrain in the Zvornik region, however your answer was sufficient enough. Within the system who is in charge of asanacija. Can you please answer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, a reference has been made to a document, an exhibit. If such references are going to be made, I think it appropriate that that document be shown to the witness or at least provided to the parties, especially when content is mentioned in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
