utterances.text: Yes. And, Mr. Stojanovic, I think your question is too general. You have to ask a specific question concerning the testimony of this witness or concerning with the specific document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Then I would kindly ask the usher to help us with Exhibit P539. I believe that my learned friends from the OTP have it. I have it in B/C/S. This is an order of the Main Staff dated 17 July 1995, and the term asanacija is mentioned under item 5. Mr. Butler, will you agree with me on that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct. I had forgotten about this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't want to insist on that. I have to bear the time in question, so I have to reduce my questions a little. However, when we were searching through all the documents, we came across this order, but I used it because of the intervention by Mr. McCloskey. My question now is: According to the rules in effect in Republika Srpska, who is in charge of carrying out asanacija in the battlefield area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- in that context, there's two answers. With respect to the rules generally, it is a rear services function because that is where the medical branch lies within. Within the general practice of the Republika Srpska, what we tend to see is that mixed military and civilian commissions will be established under the auspice of either the army or civil protection in order to accomplish a specific task of removing bodies from a battlefield area. So within the context of the Republika Srpska, there is significant involvement with respect to the municipal authorities and the civil protection people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that there was a specialised unit of the civilian protection that was a unit for asanacija which was in charge of these specific tasks?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we talking specifically July of 1995 and Zvornik, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Butler. I'm interested in July 1995 in the Zvornik area.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I'm not aware that a specific unit existed with that task.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the usher to put Exhibit D50 in front of the witness. This is a decree on the organisation and functioning of the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We had Article 27 of this decree translated. And, Mr. Butler, can we have your brief comment on this article. According to the regulations in effect in Republika Srpska on the organising and functioning of civilian protection, Article 27 prescribes the organisation of specialised units of civil protection. Under item 8 here you can see a specialised unit for asanacija. I appreciate that you have not dwelled much upon the issue of civil protection, so I'm not insisting on your broad knowledge on that. However, if this is regulated by a rule, was it then to be expected from the civilian protection in Zvornik to also have a specialised unit for asanacija in view of the fact that this was prescribed by law?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly it says - and again hopefully it's not just an issue of translation - it says may be organised, not will. With respect to Zvornik specifically, there was a large effort for asanacija as a result of large numbers of bodies which were known to be in and around the Zvornik municipality in 1992 in the latter months as a result of the combat. Again, I don't know of a specific unit organised for asanacija in July of 1995 in the Zvornik municipality. It may be there. I don't know about it or it may just be another general function of the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. We shall go on to prove that this unit did indeed exist. I believe that we have received a document from the OTP proving that there was such a unit and their structure is explained. What I would like to say here that the asanacija, that is the burial of bodies is not a crime and it is a legal and legitimate military operation and activity. I am talking within a military context, not about the legal inferences of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. There was a mention again of a document and an argument to prove something related to civil protection and asanacija which Mr. Butler has been cross-examined on. If -- when counsel does this, I think it's incumbent upon him to let Mr. Butler review the document and explain, because this is cross-examination, this is the subject he's crossing him on. Just mentioning this document and saying we're going to go on is not proper. Again, a statement regarding whether asanacija in the context of our case is legal or not is really not relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with you. Mr. Stojanovic, do you have that document? You mean that you have a document received from the OTP providing that there was such a unit and their structure is explained. What's that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't have it on me today; that's why I did not insist on it. However, we shall have an opportunity to explore it. This is a document that we received from the OTP indicating the structure of all of these units which were established pursuant to the -- to Article 27 of the legal act on the organising and functioning of civilian protection. This document indicates the structure, the number of members in the unit, and the command structure of that unit. However, I haven't got that document on me today, so I could not refer to it today. I have just received it, actually, however it hasn't been translated. So we will have to prepare this document for some other examination. It wouldn't be correct of me to continue questioning this witness on a document that hasn't been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This again brings up a very serious issue, Your Honour. Cross-examining on what I think are important subjects, I know both for Mr. Blagojevic and for Mr. Stojanovic. Bringing up things like this, leaving them hang, and not giving Mr. Butler a chance to discuss them. Mr. Butler will be available in the future, and it looks like we're going to have to call him back. But this is even more of a serious issue with Mr. Obrenovic who has been cross-examined through Mr. Butler on items that were not brought up to him or shown to him, most recently the suggestion that the duty officer of the barracks was his best man. And this may be, again, just this context of the common law system at work. And I know Mr. Stojanovic is doing his best and I think he's doing an excellent job, but this is a problem, especially in the context of Mr. Obrenovic, whose credibility has been challenged on material he has not been allowed to respond to. And Mr. Obrenovic is going to be sentenced partly based on his credibility, and I'm not exactly sure what to do at this point. But I did want to bring up that issue, and I know Mr. Stojanovic is aware of it and is doing his best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas. I hope you will be very concise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very concise, Your Honour. First of all, this technique was used by the Prosecution in their direct throughout, number one, where the gentleman was referring, there are documents, there are rules, and that's why a couple of times I intervened and we never really got from the Prosecution the documents and the rules they were referring to. Secondly, Mr. Stojanovic had a good-faith basis for making that remark. In front of a jury, obviously, it would be rather improper to do so. But we do have professional Judges, he does have a document, and I believe he's making a good-faith basis. So based on that, albeit, he shouldn't be commenting, I don't think there's anything improper of the way he's going about cross-examination, particularly in light of the rules we have here. I don't want to interfere with Mr. Stojanovic's cross, I do want to say, however, as long as he has a good-faith basis and as long as some time down the road he is going to be introducing witnesses with respect to this document it is perfectly proper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic and Mr. Karnavas knows I'm not suggesting Mr. Stojanovic is doing anything deliberately improper. I don't think that's an issue at all. However, to bring up a document that perhaps cuts against Mr. Butler's testimony or calls doubt on whether or not he sufficiently researched an issue, which comments have been made in the questioning, knowing Mr. Butler is going to be through testifying in a couple of hours and not giving Mr. Butler a chance to respond is improper. It doesn't help us get to the truth and it unfairly -- is an unfair technique of cross-examination on Mr. Butler. And I -- again, I don't think there's anything deliberate here, but it's just the way it's turned out. And I know Mr. Stojanovic has the document and I'm sure he'll tell us what it is. But we don't have any of these Defence documents now. These are the first time we're seeing the Defence documents. So that is an additional problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, taking into consideration of the time of your cross-examination, I don't think we should further pursue this issue anymore. And this Trial Chamber will attach very little weight to this section of the testimony unless in the future, Mr. Stojanovic, you have the opportunity to provide the witness with that statement or this document and unless you have another opportunity to clear it up in the future. You may move on, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I am sorry about the time, but I am giving up on insisting whether -- insisting on that at the moment. We shall see in the future whether Zvornik had such a unit of civilian protection or not. But now if you can help me and tell me how much more do I have in order to bring my cross-examination to an end?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, just a few questions about mobilisation. I would like to remind you that on the 14th of November - I don't want to show you the transcript - you said that when you say "mobilisation" you mean the engineers, Jokic, Milosevic, the Ministry of Defence. Are you able to remember that or do I need to show you that excerpt from the transcript?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- on the 14th of November -- I'd have to see that because I'm just not catching the context. I think I know what you're talking about with respect to the requisitioning of civil equipment by the military. I mean, I think that's the context we're discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I ask the usher, please, to show the 60/3 to Mr. Butler, pages 4559.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Page 4559. Within that context, I wanted to ask you the following: Within the procedure of requisitioning equipment, at any point in time in the formal sense does this require a document by the chief of engineers and is there any such document? Have you come across any such document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to the events of July of 1995, I have not come across a document which represents a formal request from the chief of engineers to the assistant commander rear services for the requisition of a civilian piece of engineering equipment. Whether in any other time that has occurred, that is not an area I have looked at in great detail, so I don't have an answer to that. But certainly in July 1995, I do not have an engineering document which reflects that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that the title of the assistant commander for personnel, organisation, and mobilisation indicates that this is the duty of a personnel officer and he is the one who addresses higher instances when a requisitioning of equipment is required?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that's accurate. With respect to personnel, he would be the one who does that. However, with respect to equipment - and I have seen some documents where they are going out to the civilian economy - it comes out of rear services and not the personnel or mobilisation. So with respect to equipment, I don't believe that that's an accurate statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But am I right when I say that in order to mobilise soldiers, so conscripts, this is something that is done through the personnel service, while the requisitioning of machinery and equipment is done through the rear services. Would that be correct, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that Mihajlo Galic, deputy commander for personnel affairs, that was his duty, and he was the person who was in charge of such tasks?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to personnel, that is correct. That is his duty. Although, I don't think it's deputy commander. I believe it's considered deputy chief of staff for personnel affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will just remind you that in the workbook of the officer on duty states for Galic to mobilise everybody. If you recall this was on the 14th or the 15th. It was at the time that Dragan Jokic was duty officer. So does that indicate to you that Galic was the one who was supposed to carry out the mobilisation within the defence ministry?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree and then I would also remind you that as you noted earlier, this same officer was at the IKM at that period and presumably would not be able to accomplish that mobilisation function.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that perhaps on the 15th or on the 14th and the 15th he did come to the command of the Zvornik Brigade, because, to say the least, that was the task of the highest priority at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to go back to the IKM logbook and it would indicate in that logbook at what point he got relieved. Again, that is something I could check. I don't know whether it was on the 14th or 15th or whether it was longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's finish, then, with the elements indicating the character of Dragan Jokic and then I plan to close with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the usher to give us a document, D52.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, did you have the opportunity earlier to see this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And I guess what I'm surprised is that we've already had this translated into English. I don't know why you guys have translated it yourself, but I have seen this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that we have the following situation here: That a group of prisoners, Muslim prisoners, from the Pilica school managed to escape on the 14th and that it was wandering in the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade and that they found themselves with this son and father Nesko Djokic. He tried to help them. He gave them food and tried to transfer them to an area under the control of the BiH army. That he was caught in that and prevented from doing so, and that the officers of the Zvornik Brigade reported him as a person who was cooperating with enemy -- with the enemy army. Am I correct when I say that, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe partially. It is my assessment with respect to this and the information the investigation has developed that the individuals, in fact, did not escape from the Pilica school on the 14th but we are individuals who survived at Branjevo Military Farm and from that location attempted to make their way out of the territory of the Zvornik Brigade towards the BH territory. I believe I discussed this issue in my narrative, where I lay out the information which supports that. But as to the greater context, yeah, the situation that you have here is where these two individuals were reported to the command of the Zvornik Brigade for essentially aiding enemy soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, in the course of your investigation and after you read Obrenovic's statement, did you have access or gain information that Dragan Jokic on the 18th of July personally demined a minefield and led five to six Muslim young men to go to the Muslim federation, and according to Obrenovic the commander of a unit of the BiH Semso Muminovic thanked them for this consideration which was extended to these young men?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe an account is found in Colonel Obrenovic's first statement to the OTP, either his first or second. I'm not exactly sure which one. But I am familiar with that general account, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that such an act at that point in time when all of that was considered to be cooperation with the enemy, this was an act of personal courage, doing something like that, demining a minefield and enabling these young men, perhaps even children, to cross into the area under the control of the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In one respect, given the lack of proper record-keeping of the minefields, anyone going in and trying to remove or demine certain areas, that's a personal act of courage, regardless of their motivation. With respect to Dragan Jokic, again I have no way of knowing whether this was an individual act or an act on orders from the superior. So I really don't believe that I can appropriately comment one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But you agree with me that it was proof of a courageous personal act at that point in time to allow a group of five to six young men to pass through?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, I mean not knowing whether it was on orders from a superior or whether it was of his own individual initiative, I don't know that I can comment one way or the other on that. I just don't know the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, are you familiar with the role of Dragan Jokic in the implementation of the Dayton Agreement and are you aware of the recognition he received from the army of the United States, Russia, the BiH army and so on after the signing of the Dayton Agreement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that the American army offered Major Jokic, precisely because his accomplishments in the implementation of the Dayton Accords and demining to receive an honourary rank and work for the American army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, do you have or did you have access at any point to a document which could link Jokic's name with the reburial operation. So I'm not talking about testimonies, I'm talking about documents.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. There is no specific document that does that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now just Exhibit D59. Could the usher please show this to the witness, and then I will be completing my cross-examination with that, Your Honours. Your Honours, this is an article in the respected BiH newspaper, Slobodna Bosna. We have provided a translation. The article is dated 11th of October, 2001, and it was written by journalist Emir Hodzic. Because we are short of time, I would like to read out the last passage, that last paragraph which we underlined which is relevant. And we would like to put that to Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So in this final part, the public and the journalist from this newspaper says: "The only certain thing is that none of those responsible for this crime was ever responsible besides Colonel Obrenovic, who was the chief of staff and who is charged with the crimes, and Dragan Jokic from Zvornik, no one has ended up in The Hague so far." And the sentence that we would like to specifically point out. "The inhabitants of Podrinje, Drina valley, had on several occasions tried to suggest to the investigators that the transfer of Dragan Jokic was a particular farce and spitting on Bosnian bones, because Jokic was an unimportant military person in the chain of command and direction, while tens of individuals responsible for ordering and carrying out the murders of civilians are still at liberty." Mr. Butler, would you agree with what the public of Bosnia and Herzegovina has said regarding Dragan Jokic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly would agree with the fact that tens, and perhaps hundreds, of individuals with respect to this are still at liberty, some indicted and some not. I don't believe that his role is unimportant. He is a part of a process. And in retrospect, it really doesn't matter what I believe in this regard. He was, in fact, indicted and he is, in fact, standing trial. His ultimate responsibility and importance I believe is an issue for the Bench and not a judgement for myself, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. And to finish with this, are you familiar with the fact that Dragan Jokic is the first active officer of the Army of Republika Srpska who voluntarily surrendered to this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I am aware of that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact, Mr. Butler, that until today he's the only officer of the VRS who has voluntarily responded to the summons by this Tribunal and who has come and surrendered to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I agree. To my knowledge, he is the only VRS officer who has voluntarily surrendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am -- I would like to conclude my cross-examination. Thank you very much. If I repeated myself in some places, I would just like you to keep in mind that I come from a different legal tradition with a different type of examination. So please take that into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think it's time for a break. We'll make a 20 minutes' break and we'll resume at 10 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, your re-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could briefly show Mr. Butler an exhibit, 248.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is an intercept dated 16 July at 1048 hours. If you could take a look at that, Mr. Butler. It talks about Kravica. It's the restoration of the terrain, the word asanacija has been used there. It hasn't been done. I've just, by nothing must be found on the road, not even a shred of cloth. Had the civilian protection rally engaged the units over there which have work obligations, et cetera. They must be cleared by 1300 hours. In fact, by 1500 hours today. Y says: "Okay, I'll pass it on. X says: "In the surrounding are everything must be done. They've just this minute come to me from higher command and asked me to do that. "Okay, understood. I'll pass it on." From this brief intercept, do you have an opinion regarding whether this is a military or civilian people involved in this intercept actually speaking on it, I mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's tough to say. The phrase "higher command" implies military as opposed to what they might say if it was the civilian leadership. But I don't believe it's real clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could this be the MUP or the civilian protection organisation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a possibility, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me go on to another subject. On the 12th and 13th of July, in your opinion were Potocari and the town of Bratunac in the Bratunac Brigade's zones of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. For the 12th and 13th of July, in your opinion were the 2nd and 3rd Infantry Battalions or the elements of them that have been identified in Potocari taken away from the command of Vidoje Blagojevic in any way?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I have no evidence that suggests that. I believe that they're still under his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In your opinion, were the elements of the Bratunac Brigade MPs on the 12th and 13th of July in Potocari taken away from or hijacked in some manner from the command of Vidoje Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. The fact that Captain First Class Momir Nikolic is working on controlling their activities is a function of the command of Blagojevic, not an isolation of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In your opinion, did Vidoje Blagojevic have any responsibility in the sense of military responsibility to the able-bodied Muslim men separated in Potocari and detained also in Bratunac, including the men that were put there from along the road?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the relevant brigade commander, I believe that he did have a military responsibility with respect to their -- not only guarding them, as he should be doing, but also to their proper treatment, medical treatment, and other aspects of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you believe that Momir Nikolic was removed from the command responsibility of Vidoje Blagojevic in some way in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall from your review of the investigation the incident of a survivor of the Jadar River?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you -- very briefly, I don't want to take more than about five more minutes, if I can, can you tell us what you recall about the specific facts of that case and whether or not there are any elements of possible organisation from a higher command involved in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At this point I would like the Prosecutor to name who this witness is, give a code or whatever, and whether this witness will be testifying, because now we're having Mr. Butler trying to sum up what this particular individual might have said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm surprised, Your Honour. This man is in evidence under 92 bis. He's the one Jadar River survivor. He is part of the indictment. I tried -- I don't remember his name at the moment, but I can come up with it. He's in the evidence already. He has been accepted as 92 bis. It's a very distinctive story and I can -- Witness P175. I do have his name if we want to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I don't think so. You may proceed -- yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: My only concern, Your Honour, at this point, now that I know who he's talking about -- my concern is why do we have Mr. Butler commenting about the individual's statement? If he wants to -- you know, perhaps the question, I think, should be rephrased so we know exactly what it is that he's asking Mr. Butler to speak about. I'm assuming that there has been no contact, and so from the question that is being posed, I don't see how Mr. Butler can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think Mr. McCloskey has asked about the elements of the organisation from the higher commander involved in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. It was brought up regarding the Cerska Valley, Your Honour, so I was just bringing it up which I think from this -- well, the relevance should become clear or lack thereof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you just give us briefly what you recall about what that witness as now part of this trial record has said and just the briefest highlights?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect, he indicates notwithstanding the issues to his capture that any point in time just before or at noon on 13 July, him and a group of other people who were being held at Konjevic Polje are put on a bus, driven to a location at the Jadar River. They are taken off the bus and then they are subsequently executed at that location, with the exception, of course, of that individual. The indication that I have with respect to organisation is the fact that at a point in time where the buses were being used primarily to move the Bosnian Muslims out of Potocari, starting at that point and then going further to Cerska and then even further in time on the 13th where you start seeing buses starting to now load up with Bosnian Muslim men along Sandici, for me that's a point where we start seeing the transition from the buses just carrying Bosnian Muslims from Potocari and are now starting to be directed to start loading Bosnian Muslim males who are being captured from the column and now are starting to be used directly with respect to the prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, in your research did you have any indication that the VRS investigated abuses of Muslim men from Srebrenica under the military rules that you have already gone over in detail?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. The reports from the relevant military Prosecutor's offices and the military court systems have no data that suggests that the VRS began any form of investigations with respect to any of these abuses. I understand that the investigation has talked to a number of the Prosecutors and Judges, and they have confirmed what the records indicate, that there were no cases where this was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you, in that same review, found any indication that any VRS or MUP for that matter troops have been punished in any way for abusing the Muslims from Srebrenica in 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I found nothing to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, given the time constraints we're under, I don't need to ask any more questions. I would rather turn it over to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions from Judges? Judge Vassylenko, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, to the extent you can tell us: Where did you work and what positions did you hold during the time of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and particularly during the critical time relevant for this case.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to my background during the war in Bosnia, I left my European assignment in August of 1992. I was then assigned to a unit in the United States, United States 3rd Army. Its geographic area of responsibility was south-west Asia and the Middle East. And from August 1992 through my being assigned here in April of 1997, my geographic focus was south-west Asia and the Middle East. Specifically in July of 1995 I was rather active during that period doing shift work, because the July and August 1995 time frame generally corresponded with the height of the summer training summer of the Iraqi army, and they had a rather annoying tendency to practice rather close to the Kuwaiti boarder. Given my job responsibility at the time, it was something that I had to keep great track of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Butler, do you know the meaning of the word "Krivaja"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Krivaja is a small creek or stream that actually runs through an area of the Zvornik municipality in part and I think also the Birac municipality. That's the only connotation I know of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: So the operation was named Krivaja 95 due to the name of this small creek, yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that was the case. I don't believe there's another meaning associated with it, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, during your testimony and during the testimony of other witnesses, very often such terms as deputy commander and assistant commander were used as interchangeable.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They should not be. They're within the rules as well as in the practical application of the framework. The only individual who performs a function of deputy commander is the chief of staff. There are -- however, within the framework of the brigade and of the corps, there are three other individuals who are known as assistant commanders. The terms are not interchangeable, however.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. And then the terms "assistant commander" and "chief," for example, for security and intelligence or "chief of engineering" or "chief of personnel" also was used as interchangeable or at least as equal terms in regard to the position of the person who has this position.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that instance with respect to the chief of security, because he is one of the designated assistant commanders, that is -- the formal term is the assistant for security or intelligence affairs if it's light infantry brigade. When the phrase "chief of engineering" or "chief of intelligence" is used, the formal phrase should be the assistant chief of staff for engineering or assistant chief of staff for intelligence. That reflects the fact that engineering and intelligence fall under the operative branch under the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: What rank would an assistant commander in the brigade staff typically have in normal circumstances?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In normal circumstances, I believe the position codes for the assistant commanders are lieutenant colonel and perhaps colonel. The brigade commander's rank should be colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. In your work on this and the Krstic case, did you have access to the intercepts of communications for both sides from NATO forces.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. We don't have access to that material. The only material that we have access to are those from the ABiH, which we have relevant to the searches and the cooperation. We also have some intercepts which were derived with respect to the VRS's intercepts of ABiH communications, which were seized documents. But we have no outside intercepts which we could use to corroborate or anything of that nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: While studying the Bosnian Muslim intercepts of the VRS communications, did you anticipate any deception in conversation, knowing that the VRS was aware it was listened in to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And again, there was in the Krstic case -- I answered this in some depth. The issue with deception is limited generally to the object of trying to draw the attention of the person listening or his intelligence organs away from the true objective of what you're trying to accomplish or not accomplish. The problem with deception, at least with respect to the overall time of context, is that while it is possible to deceive an opponent for perhaps a day or a week or several weeks, at a point in time it becomes clear as events unfold and events occur that you either have been deceived or that the information you're getting is valid. So with respect to looking for or looking at evidence of whether or not the VRS was attempting at the low level to deceive deliberately the ABiH with respect to the military operations were on the ground, I looked at that and I saw no evidence of it. On the larger scale, again looking at those intercepts, particularly having the advantage now that we also have the military documents and understanding the greater context, to see whether it's part of a deception with respect to the VRS's communications even with relation to the crime, and it becomes quite clear that they're not. The context -- so in that respect, and I will leave again in the Krstic transcript the much longer discussion that I had on that. But yes, I mean, not only from the fact that we might be deceived with respect to what the ABiH was giving us, but I also did take into account a potential deception that the VRS itself was attempting to play on to the ABiH intelligence organs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: So some information in intercepts was false?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I believe that because of the time and the circumstances involved, there were not instances where the information that was being imparted by the VRS was part of a deliberate deception. There are certainly instances where when you look at the context of what happens that some subscribers who are talking on the phones -- or the radio telephones don't know what they're talking about or don't understand the greater context. But again, deception is not random. Deception is designed for a military purpose to draw somebody's attention away from somewhere. And that is not what I see. I do not see the evidence of a deliberate military campaign with respect to telecommunications to draw the ABiH's attention away from Zepa or away from the military battlefield that's occurring in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: My next question: When studying the documents, did you notice any discrepancies between the intercepts and the combat reports related to the critical period?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe with respect to the intercepts and the combat reports, I believe they dovetail fairly well within context. Certainly, again, there will be come instances where some correspondents may or may not know what's being talked about. But I think that you can do a very good job - and I believe I've done so certainly in my report, if not necessarily in my testimony - of being able to dovetail within the broader military context the intercepts and how they favourably compare to the events that the VRS itself is describing on the ground. Again, a lot of it doesn't get normally explored because within the constraints of time and the case itself, many of the things that are legitimate military acts are there and understood and are just not a part of the case. But on an overall level, I think they do dovetail quite well with the combat reports and the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Could you indicate the whereabouts of Colonel Blagojevic during the period of 11 through 17 July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my understanding that for the most part he was in and around his headquarter's location. Based on conflicting witness statements to the OTP, I don't want to speculate where on the ground he was at any given time. I'm not sure that would be fair to the accused. And given the fact that many of those people may well have reason to misrepresent parts of their testimony or their statement because of their own liability, I wouldn't want to speculate about that. However, I think the greater body of information does at least place Colonel Blagojevic in and around his headquarters during that period. I have no information that would indicate that he was either ill or physically absent in another place. And again, after 13 July when he sends his chief of staff to command its command detachment towards Zepa, it would place an additional onus on him as a commander to be available to make those key decisions. So I think that's about as far as I can go with respect to what I do know about the subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Could you indicate the whereabouts of Major Jokic during the same period?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Jokic, again during the same period, I believe his whereabouts are well-corroborated with respect to the Zvornik Brigade list which shows the daily whereabouts of the brigade command and staff. And certainly from the period of the 13th and 14th on, I believe his whereabouts are well-documented, again in and around the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade. Again, I would default back to that document for the broad ones. Certainly we do have the same problem with various witness statements and testimony which conflict on that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Have you come across any specific facts proving direct and active participation of Colonel Blagojevic in the murder operation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Nothing that would be something I can look at and say a direct fact. Most of what I believe I've laid out in my narrative are the inference based on the events occurring at his command. And to be clear, there is no direct document, certainly one that I would equate to the 15 July interim combat report by Colonel Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Judge Argibay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Yes. Only questions of clarification, Mr. Butler. As far as I can recall, we had by the beginning of July three kinds of police around that -- I mean the military police, the MUP and the special police. But on the 10th of July, this order by Mr. Tomislav Kovac assigning Mr. Borovcanin as a MUP unit commander with these units that compromise special police detachment, mixed company of joint MUP forces and a company from the Jahorina training centre. Do you remember that document, that's P157.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: So Mr. Borovcanin was a MUP commander.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, he was the deputy commander of the special police brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: So we can just join the special police brigade with the MUP and tell that we have at this point in time, 10 July, 1995, military police and MUP. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. Within the MUP categories, they're broken down into -- and maybe what will make it a little less confusing. Within the broader category of the MUP police, you have the special police brigade and you have the companies that are organised by the local CSBs or centres for security. So those are the two broad families of the MUP police. The third instance that you had mentioned, the police trainees from Jahorina, I think on the basis of whom they're being ordered to go with would probably, if you had to lump them into category, you would lump them with the special police assets under Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay. That brings the other two clarification questions in hand. When you were asked about this famous intercept, P203, between a general and Jankovic, and this is in the transcript of the 18th November, in the cross-examination, you said that you've changed from considering that that was Colonel Jankovic of the Main Staff to a MUP police officer Jankovic. That's in the transcript. And I wanted to ask you: When he said he is police commander Jankovic, couldn't he have been military police at the time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with yours. I don't recall saying the MUP police officer Jankovic. I hope it's the military police Jankovic. If I said that, I misstated it. And to clarify, it's the military police, not the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay. Always in the intercepts then we have this intercept that is identified as P217 where someone calling from General Krstic is looking for Ljubisa. And I remember or recall that you said he was looking for Borovcanin. Couldn't it be that he was looking for Beara?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I hold that open as a possibility, I think the most reasonable possibility with that respect is because there is a conversation between General Krstic and Borovcanin less than 30 minutes later, that is the most probable identification. While I hold open that possibility that he might be looking for Colonel Beara, presumably as Colonel Beara was in Bratunac on the 14th of July, at that time, if he was in the building they should have been able to locate him if that was the intent. So, like I said, I believe it's Borovcanin, but I hold open that other possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay. And to finish with a question of the intercepts. In the intercept that's marked P244, that's the conversation between Zivanovic and Beara, can you or do you have an explanation for why Beara didn't know that Zivanovic was no more the chief commander of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am, I don't have an explanation for that. That is something that in my mind that does remain an open question. One would think that it would be likely that he would be aware of that fact, and it remains something to this day that I cannot explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I abandon the intercepts and I have two more clarification questions. We have this report by Mr. Vasic on the 13th July, 1995, telling about the meeting held this morning with General Mladic and saying that all the other tasks and there was this discussion that said he's yielding all other tasks to MUP, or whatever the word is. But I'm not concerned with the words. I do want to ask you if you remember P539, I think that's the order of General Mladic, that's on the 17th July, 1995. This integration of operation to crush lagging Muslim forces. Do you recall that document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay. Isn't there something that isn't very consistent on the 13th of July Mr. Vasic said that everything is on the hands of the MUP. And then on the 17th, General Mladic is also talking about MUP with other members of the army forces?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, ma'am. And as I've indicated in my testimony, I believe that while Vasic is reporting to his superiors his view of the situation, as I've indicated, his forces certainly were not alone on that road or in the greater context of the sweep operations. What's also missing between the 13th Vasic order and the 17th order from Mladic is the 15 July and 16 July pieces of evidence, the one from Colonel Milanovic indicating that based on the current situation and forces that are being moved around, they want the Bratunac Brigade commander to assume command of all of the army and MUP forces along that road. And that is a reflection in the daily combat report of 16 July, that Colonel Blagojevic is taking the actions that are consistent with that. So I think those are the missing pieces in the context. And then when you get to the 17th July, now that Colonel Blagojevic is going with a unit of his towards Zepa, there again is a vacuum within the command framework, and somebody from the Main Staff is now appointed to oversee those operations. But I think if you look at it from the 13th through the 17th, while at various times the commander of that small operation changes, the actual conduct of the operation and the fact that all of the elements that are participating are coordinating their activities doesn't change. That is a consistent from the 13th to the 17th. It is just at what echelon it's being controlled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay. My last question. This is a clarification from one of the questions of Mr. Karnavas. I think when there was different forces working on this search of the terrain, and you were asked about the difficulties of two different quarters or three just having the same area. This order of the 13th July 1995 by General Krstic, and this is Exhibit P472, do you recall that order?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Point 5 says: "Men who participate in the search of the terrain will wear a white band on their right shoulders as an identification mark." Could that be an order also to the MUP personnel who was at that time working at that place?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the unique aspects of this particular conflict, given the fact that the parties of the conflict physically look the same, they talk the same, they wore the same uniforms, was that within the VRS there was the practice of coloured ribbons on various locations of a uniform on any given day so they could identify friend from foe at distance. Now, that order is specifically directed to the military formations. The logical assumption should be that the MUP forces as well as the non-Drina Corps military forces, the 65th Protection Regiment military police, who were also as part of those operations, the logical assumption would be that they too would have received the orders to do that. We don't have an order that reflects that, either in the terms of a verbal intercept or a documentary order to any of those units. So I agree it is a logical assumption that they would, in fact, do that. I just don't know that with respect to the MUP and with respect to the military police of the 65th Protection Regiment that it was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Butler, did you testify this morning in the Krstic case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you make any corrections concerning the mistakes in the transcript of this case, the Blagojevic case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were three specific areas of the testimony that they were introducing which I indicated were corrections. In two of the three instances, the name Obrenovic was transcribed when, in fact, the individual we were discussing was Erdemovic. And in the third instance there was one particular passage that was attributed to the witness which, in fact, it is my understanding that is a comment to the Court from Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just for the information of the parties, those three places are in the transcript, page 5.412, line 16, page 5.406, line 14, and page 5.376, line 19. This Trial Chamber would like to take the testimony of Mr. Butler this morning concerning the correction of those places into the evidence of this case through 92 bis. Any questioning concerning of the Judges' questions? Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just perhaps a clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, regarding the conversation between when General Krstic was looking for Ljubisa, I think you stated on the record that on the 14th of July that Beara was in Bratunac. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That should be 13 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And did you have a chance to review your entire testimony in this case prior to speaking to the Appellant Chamber?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I reviewed was the passages that the Defence wanted to introduce. I am currently going now through the volume of my testimony trying to determine if there are any errors in that. But I have not read through the entire volume of my testimony yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just ask that because there may be more to come on the corrections, of course. And I have nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have one maybe two corrections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, when you were testifying this morning, and had I known I would have been there watching it, when you were testifying, did the famous "up there" intercept come into play?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The intercept in that respect was -- we didn't talk about it. It was part of the written submissions of the transcript. And I indicated that with the exception of three minor transcription errors, that I adopted that in full.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Adopted that portion of the testimony --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That is --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The three that were introduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I guess my question is: You adopted your portion of the testimony in this case, and that is that since the Krstic case there's been other testimony that has come into light with respect to who might have -- how to interpret that particular intercept as it relates to the killings that occurred in Branjevo Farm on the 16th. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. But again, what was said in this particular case was -- I affirmed, there was no additional discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no questions which would arise from all the previous questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, the most difficult part is the admission of the documents. Mr. McCloskey, are there any documents -- of course there are so many documents to tender through Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I have a list that everybody else has, and it's an 11-page list. And I would just offer that material. But along with it as a declaration of the current team leader of team 6 that acknowledges that he's gone over this list and researched the records and that this list identifying the various places where the documents came from is correct. I believe Mr. Butler assisted in that process. I did not remember to ask Mr. Butler about that. So I believe this list that I'm providing you reflects all of the exhibits that have been referred to and where the Prosecution got them. And with that foundation and with Mr. Butler's testimony and with the various documents as we've discussed them, I would offer all these documents into evidence. And I'm not aware of any problem regarding that with the Defence. We haven't had a real chance to talk about it, so there may have been something. But I would guess between me and the Defence we could work out any issues, and I don't know if they've had time to look over this long list either. So that's -- I don't think we need to bring in Alistair Graham. If the Defence would accept the declaration as a stipulation under the Rules, but we can of course do that if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You see, my question to you is is there any stop in the sequence of those numbers?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Ms. Stewart's the expert on that, and there probably is. We never can get things perfect in terms of sequence and there are gaps. We can have those identified if that would be helpful. And I'm sure with a little more study, we can identify potential gaps. We sometimes leave gaps to fill in things. So that would be normal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. Can you do it now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I mean, just for the sake of the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sure Ms. Stewart can do it, and perhaps if we could just have a minute or two, she will be able to get back to me on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Any objections, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. The list is quite comprehensive. As Mr. Butler was testifying and referring to documents, I don't recall anything that at least I had objections to with respect to the admissibility, perhaps as far as the weight is concerned. We were handed this list rather -- this afternoon. It is comprehensive. I do take Mr. Alistair Graham's word. His signature is on it, I would assume that he's an honourable man and would do the right thing. And so I have no problems with that. I would ask that I be given an opportunity to look over this list over the next couple of days in great detail just to be on the safe side. If there is something, I obviously would bring it to the Prosecution's attention first, see if there's anything that we can resolve. But frankly, from the looks of it, it would appear that on face value I have no problems with the admissibility of any of this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Stojanovic, do you have any objections to the admission of those documents into the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have gone over the list of exhibits which the Prosecution wishes to tender through the testimony of Mr. Butler. And in principle, if you give time to Mr. Karnavas, then I would also use that time so that I could also express my position. But if you think that we need to express our position today, I would like to say the following: For understandable reasons given previously, this Defence is opposed to admitting any exhibit which refers to or relates to the intercepts. Because we believe that this is still a topic that needs to be discussed further. Also, we do not wish exhibits to be tendered, the following exhibits: P507 and P509 and P534 for the reasons we previously stated relating to the possession of these exhibits and also the fact that they were handed in shortly prior to the beginning of trial by Mr. Obrenovic. So the chain of custody of these documents for those reasons and the possibility of manipulation of these documents. As far as the other exhibits being tendered here, and in view of our own defence and in view of the fact how many of these documents even refer to the role of Dragan Jokic or the role of the engineering of the Zvornik Brigade, so to the extent that is mentioned we will not have any major objections for any of these exhibits to be admitted. Because we are not contesting any of them. In any case, the list that we received from the Prosecution when we received the documents that are to be tendered, which was a month ago, we hope that we can state our position. As far as the exhibits we received today, I am not in a position right now to go from one exhibit to the next, but I believe that it's the same list and that the exhibits on the list are the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I didn't find that document P534. Maybe it's located somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it -- I thought I found it, but now -- yes, it is. It's a bit out of sequence. It's after 520.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Oh, yes, on page 9?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Page 9. I don't know how I found it, but that's where it's sitting. And just one clarification for Mr. Stojanovic, Exhibit 509 is the IKM or forward command post operations duty logbook. And that was actually seized from the Zvornik Brigade back in the search, I think has Mr. Butler has testified. In addition, I should say that Mr. Graham's list stating where these things came from in his declaration is Exhibit P356.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, concerning the documents and the comments made by the parties, this Bench would like to give three days to the parties to review this very comprehensive list. And if there is any objections, I hope the Defence team would file their submissions next Monday. So if the time limit is passed, this Trial Chamber will take the actions. Is that agreeable to the parties, taking into consideration that tomorrow and Friday we are not going to sit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I have the answer to your previous question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And for the record, the following exhibits were left blank: Number 373; number 418; 420 through 422; 429 through 433; 436 through 438; 454 through 455; 460 through 463; and 473 through 475.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, let's deal with the Defence team's exhibits. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You have to inform me which document we have to work on, because it seems to me that almost every day we got a new list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But you will be pleased to note, Your Honour -- you will be very pleased to note that I have been able to fit them all on less than one page, the ones that I wish to introduce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: These -- the ones that we wish to introduce, Your Honour, are D77, D78, and D79. These are the photographs from the Krstic case, as you may recall. Then it would be D80 and D81; those were the transcripts from the witnesses that I questioned Mr. Butler with respect to his interrogative techniques, good guy, bad guy, one was where he played sort of the bad guy and then another one, the good guy. Then D82 is the excerpts from the brigade rules. D83, excerpts from the transcript on page 55, line 1, to page 56 line 3. D84, the manual for the work command and staffs, the relevant paragraphs. And D85 rules of security service organs in the armed forces of the SFRJ, paragraph 83. So that's all, Your Honour. It's very modest, as you can see, and very relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The OTP interviews D80 and D81 of these two people are not admissible under any Rule and are not relevant. They were used to cross-examine Mr. Butler, which is fine. And the excerpt from the transcript, perhaps Mr. Karnavas can tell us what transcript that's from and what the relevance of that is, if he remembers. I -- again, transcripts are -- it's possible, but I don't see how that comes into play.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, concerning the transcript, I think if it's from another case, we could take that into consideration. But if it's from this case, I don't think it's necessary. Maybe Mr. Karnavas could shed some light on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, as you might recall, we took -- or I took a couple of questions and a couple of answers and we sort of dissected them, this was of the witness's testimony, in order to demonstrate the lack of substance and in the answer itself given the filler words. I do think that in light of -- even though they are part of the original transcript that it is the gentleman's -- my questions and his answers, I think that that is an instructive piece of evidence, because we took apart those questions and answers. And I think when it comes time to perhaps review that part of the transcript at the end of the trial which we think is relevant in determining or deciphering some of the answers given by this particular gentleman, I think it would be very useful to have that, because we did not read it back into the record. So I know it's a little bit unusual, but nonetheless I don't think it is harmful to the Prosecution's case. As far as the statements that I wanted to introduce, D80 and D81, first of all, it is proper. You can introduce them. Whether they should or should not, that's another question. And I don't want to be giving lectures on evidence to the Prosecution at this point. However, there were some excerpts from those particular conversations. We would be willing to accept at least those pages that we made references to, because my memory is a little bit fading away as to whether I read the entire question and answer process. But at least the two pages or three pages of each transcript should be admitted into evidence. Again, I think it would be instructive. In the alternative, if of course I read the entire question and the entire answer, then it would be superfluous. But I do want to stress that there's no such thing as not being able to get this kind of evidence. Particularly in light of the Rules of Evidence where hearsay is admissible in this particular case, and the witness has been given the opportunity to be confronted on that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, at this stage, I think the document D77, D78, D79, D82, D84, and D85 are admitted into the evidence. As for the document D83, we have very serious doubts about this method to dissect the transcript. I quite agree with you Mr. Karnavas that that is a very constructive way to deal with the evidence, but we have to know the whole picture of the transcript. So D83 is not admitted into the evidence. But your questions and your submissions are all in the transcript and we'll take that into consideration. As for D80 and D81, as a general practice, those conversations or interviews with a witness or suspect are not admitted into the evidence. So those two documents, D80 and D81 are not admitted. I was informed by the Court Deputy that D77, D78, and D79 should be under seal, since there are some writings there. It is so decided. Now I turn to the Defence team of Mr. Jokic. Yes. Do you have any documents to tender, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We would like to tender D39/3, that is the takeover of duty record. Then D41/3, that is Rule 21 of the engineering company or platoon. Then the relevant parts of the statement, it is up to you to decide whether this is admissible or not, by the witness Nenad Simic, this is D44, when he is talking about his personal presence and the presence of other officers in the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade. D45, only the relevant page of the interview given by Ljubo Bojanovic. And D47/1 and /2, only the relevant parts of the statement given by Dragan Jevtic about the command of the engineering company and the presence of the commander. We also would like to tender D50, the Official Gazette of Republika Srpska, in which Article 27 of the degree on the organisation and functioning of the civilian protection was published. D52, information on cooperation with the enemy compiled and sent to the military Prosecution in Bijeljina by assistant commander Dragan Nikolic. D53, an excerpt from -- no, we don't want to tender D53. Then D57 and D58, those are definitions published in the military lexicon. D59, an article published in the Slobodna Bosna weekly in Sarajevo. That would be all that we wish to tender according to our list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Just to go through those again, D39 appears to be some sort of a record regarding transfer of duty between a guy named Lackovic and Dragan Jokic. There has been no authentication, or no foundation for that document. And while it doesn't seem like a big deal, I just don't want to start accepting documents out of the blue like this without some sort of foundation. I may be able to work this out with Mr. Stojanovic. As I said, we haven't seen this documents before. The combat rules -- and going to D41, the combat rules for engineering, Mr. Stojanovic was kind enough to give us those books so we could photocopy them, and that's no problem. D44, the interview with Nenad Simic, I would object for the same grounds I objected regarding Mr. Karnavas's interview statements. Same thing with D47 the interview with Dragan Jevtic. Same thing with D47 OTP information report. D50, the Official Gazette that was made reference to. These gazettes have not been readily available over the years. I think we have a lot more than we used to. And again there hasn't been any foundation for that. I think speaking to Mr. Stojanovic we can work that out and I want to make sure I get the complete collection of the gazettes, so if there's any related rules or statutes we take a look at that. I don't see that as a problem. D52 is no problem. That's a document that we did seize. D57 and 58, from the 1969 military lexicon, no problem, though we do have the same military lexicon a little more recent version we may take a look at to see if there's any differences. And the article from Slobodna Bosna I would object to as to relevance and probative value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. As for the document D39, it's very difficult for the Trial Chamber to make a decision at this moment. And I hope after this sitting tomorrow or any day before Monday the parties could meet to solve the problem that is raised by the Prosecution. And if there is any result, I hope -- if there's still some objections, the Prosecution should file something against it. And if there is no problem, I hope that Mr. Stojanovic could inform us about the consultations between you and the Prosecution. So we have this document pending with the Prosecution's documents. The D41/3 is admitted into the evidence. D44, D45, D46, D47/1, and D47/2, as a rule they are not admitted into the evidence. As for D50, we don't think there's any problem with this document with the Official Gazette. Generally speaking, this Trial Chamber will take these kind of official document into the evidence. So this document is admitted into the evidence. As for the D52 is admitted into the evidence. D57, D58, these two documents are admitted into the evidence. As for D59, on this document we agree with the Prosecution. We don't see much relevance to this particular case or through this witness. At this moment, we will not admit it into the evidence, and maybe in the future in the Defence case they still have the opportunity to re-tender it if the relevancy is established in a more proper way. It is so decided. Yes Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President, I know it's late.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just one other matter. There was a document D17 which was a Bratunac Brigade report allegedly drafted or executed by Mr. Blagojevic that was provided by the Defence. Mr. Butler talked about it at some length I think. And we still don't have any record of where it came from. And I think Mr. Butler testified a bit about that. And I don't know if -- I know counsel has been very busy, and they may not have been able to track down where it came from, but that is a document that Mr. Butler has talked about that is still up in the air and maybe they can shed some light on it as well. I think Mr. Butler did say it looked okay to him, but that's about all we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, to my understanding that the Defence did not tender this document, am I right, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. Although it's -- the Prosecutor is either being mistaken or -- I won't go -- where I believe he's going, but Mr. Butler did discuss it extensively and found that he had no problems with that particular document we have not tendered. But nonetheless I believe if we look at Mr. Butler's testimony and put it into context, as he likes to put it, with what was happening on the ground and with the order that was issued by the Drina Corps of July 2nd, if we put it into that general context and we look at Mr. Butler's testimony, it would appear that Mr. Butler himself laid adequate foundation for that particular document to be admitted. But the answer to your question, Your Honour, the long and short of it is: No, we haven't tendered it yet, but we are discussing it quite a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, that document was tendered on 25/09/03 through the testimony of Mr. Nikolic. And that's why I bring it up, because Mr. Butler has talked about it. I was just hoping there was some further research on the document and its origins to help us out, as I will quote my learned colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We are searching and we have been rather busy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think this Bench made a ruling that once the proper foundation is established, this document could be admitted into the evidence. I think we made that ruling somewhere on the 1st of October. But this issue is still pending, as I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I do understand that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, Mr. Butler, thank you very much indeed for coming to The Hague to give your testimony. It's really a quite long period of time. And we wish you to have a pleasant journey back home and have a pleasant Thanksgiving. I hope there's some turkey left.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three growing boys, I'm not optimistic. But thank you very much, sir, it has been a privilege to testify before this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think the hearing is adjourned. We'll meet next Monday.
